newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says EU payment systems on track for EMU start.
newsitem.headline: EMI says EU payment systems on track for EMU start.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the European Central Bank, said on Thursday that banks' payment systems would conform to minimum standards in time for the launch of a single European currency.

In a report looking at developments in this area in 1996, the EMI concluded that 10 basic principles it had set out for EU member states' domestic payment systems in 1993 had "to a great extent been met".
"Work is in progress in all EU member states which is expected to ensure full compliance with them by the start of Stage Three of European monetary union," the EMI said.

Work still had to be done in particular in making EU interbank funds transfer systems conform with the principles laid out -- which are aimed at ensuring the smooth-functioning of payments throughout the single currency area -- the EMI said.

Some countries still had work to do in implementing domestic real time gross settlement systems (RTGS), which will ultimately form the basis for access to the intra-Europe gross payment system TARGET, it said.
Further conformity was needed on legal issues, to reduce systemic risks, and on technical issues.
The report said that implementation of RTGS systems continued to be seen as a top priority by both the EU central banks and the EMI.

In February 1997, RTGS systems were fully operational in eight of the 15 EU countries. Three of these, in Belgium, Britain and Portugal, came into operation in 1996, while Ireland launched its system in February 1997, the report said.
"It is now expected that new or redesigned RTGS systems will be implemented in almost all EU countries by the end of 1997," the EMI said.
"Cooperation will have to continue between credit institutions and central banks to avoid delays in the implementation of these systems," it added.
